# Technical Writing Style Guide

## The five rules that matter most

Read these first. They are the whole guide in five lines, and they are non-negotiable on every piece this
repo publishes. Everything below is the detail behind them.

1. **No clever declarative sentences.** If a quotable-sounding line has no fact you can point at, cut it.
   Keep the number, drop the flourish. ("The fourth row settles it" is out.)
2. **Name every referent.** No dangling noun. "All four write SQL" and "the best editor of the four" make
   the reader ask "four what". Name the thing in the sentence that uses it.
3. **Exact number or plain scope, never a vague count.** "13+ data platforms" makes the reader ask "is that
   14 or 200". Say "any data platform or cloud database", or a real number.
4. **One idea per sentence, and no contradiction.** Do not fuse two facts into one sentence, and never let a
   sentence contradict the one before it.
5. **Write two reading levels down. This is not marketing copy.** Keep the technical terms, simplify the
   words around them. Dry, accurate, concise.

The test that finds all five: read a sentence and ask "what are you trying to say?", then say that in fewer,
smaller words. Also cut any filler transition and any sentence whose subject is the article, the table or the
paragraph. Inform, do not narrate.

Section 0 is the full reader-first list, section 2 has the worked before-and-after examples.

---

**Scope: every word this repo publishes.** Listicles, product highlights, blog posts, landing-page copy,
docs and release notes all follow this file. Load it before you write or edit any of them.

Three sources feed it and they do not conflict: the freeCodeCamp publication style guide (vendored at
`content/listicles/review/sources/freecodecamp-publication-style-guide.md`), the Altimate tone-of-voice guide
at `altimate-marketing-os/about-company-context/brand-messaging/tone-of-voice.md`, and the machine-checked
slop rules in `D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\slop\slop_rules.py`.


**The freeCodeCamp guide is a fallback, and its contents are guidelines rather than rules.** It is somebody
else's house style, written for a different publication and a different audience. Consult it where this file
is silent, and treat what it says as a sensible default rather than a requirement. Where it disagrees with
this file or with the tone-of-voice guide, those win and no note is needed. Nothing in it is enforced by a
gate, and no review should cite it as grounds for a change.

> **UNRESOLVED-D-DRIVE, procedural.** Raised 21 Aug 2026. The slop scorer lives on one contributor's
> Windows machine, so nobody else can run it: not another author, not macOS, not CI. Every other item on the
> mechanical bar is checkable by anyone with the repo. This one is not, which means "passes slop at CRIT 0"
> is a claim only its author can make and nobody can verify. The same is true of `slop_rules.py`, cited as a
> source feeding this guide, whose contents no reviewer outside that machine has read. Resolve it by
> vendoring the scorer and its rules into a repo, or by removing it from the mechanical bar. Until then,
> treat a skipped slop run as an expected gap rather than a failure, and say so in the PR.

Where this file and a harness disagree, the harness wins on structure and this file wins on prose. A listicle
still needs its short-version callout and a highlight still needs its byline line, because those are shape
rules the gates enforce. How the sentences inside them read is decided here.

**This file is mirrored to `D:\Atharva\NOTES\DIGITAL TWIN\Technical Writing Style Guide.md`**, which governs
technical writing in the vault. The two are the same document. Edit this copy, then run:

```bash
cp ".claude/WRITING-STYLE-GUIDE.md" "D:/Atharva/NOTES/DIGITAL TWIN/Technical Writing Style Guide.md"
```

Our target reader is a data engineer or an analytics engineer with a live problem and little patience.  Stick to a succinct, technically precise tone of voice.  Avoid aphorisms, similes, metaphores, or attempts to be smart.  Simple language is always better, but do not dumb down the technical details.  Assume the reader in a proficient engineer.

---

## 0. The reader-first rules, non-negotiable

Set by the owner on 19 Aug 2026 after reading the listicle cluster line by line. These outrank taste and
apply to every piece this repo publishes, not only listicles. Several are elaborated in the numbered sections
below and are repeated here because a reviewer reads this list first. Where a rule points at a section, that
section is the detail.

1. **Write plain English.** No flowery sentences, ever. This is the rule the other fourteen serve.
2. **No metaphors and no rhetorical flourish.** Say the literal action. A term of art with an agreed meaning (blast radius, fan-out, guardrail) is not a metaphor and stays.
3. **Never write a sentence about the article.** No "a table follows", "read this with that in mind", "here is the honest limit". Inform, do not narrate. See section 2.
4. **No self-criticism as a hook.** Do not lead with our own weakness, stage it as a reveal, or give it a heading. State a real limit plainly when the reader needs it, then move on.
5. **No bragging.** Do not tell the reader how special we are ("the data nobody else publishes"). Show the number and let it speak.
6. **No unstructured statistic dumps.** A run of numbers is a table or a bullet list, or it does not go in.
7. **Headings tell, they do not tease.** The reader must know what the section covers from the heading alone. No curiosity teasers, bare noun phrases, count riddles, dangling pronouns or aphorisms. Do not bury the lede. See section 4.
8. **Every compared item gets the same block, in the same order:** what it is, who it is for, who uses it today, the features, the pricing, what it lacks. The reader compares across items, not across four different essays.
9. **Use bullets with a bold label, then expand.** One bullet per attribute, label first. Do not bury an attribute mid-paragraph: a reader comparing several items reads down the bold labels to find the one they care about, and cannot do that if pricing is a bullet under one item and a clause under the next.
10. **Comparison tables use marks, not words.** A tick, a cross, or a hyphen for none, with a short qualifier beside the mark. Never "Yes / No / none published".
11. **Lead with use case, not benchmarks.** Fit and features are the main focus, score is secondary evidence, never the structure of the piece.
12. **Cut corporate trivia, but reference solution owners or maintainers.** No mergers, acquisitions, funding rounds or valuations. A data engineer choosing a tool does not care.  Do mention the organization behind a tool or open source project.
13. **Publish the figure, not its provenance.** Drop "who ran it", the provenance and the benchmark dates as details in the running text. Keep the number and its just link to its source.
14. **Write for the reader, not for yourself or an internal team mate.** No leaked internal identifiers, no "that third line is why...", nothing that makes them scroll back to follow the point.
15. **Open with a real introduction.** Establish context quicly to orient the reader and confirm the topic. Start with the reader's situation, demonstrate empathy, show you can relate, then say what you compare and on what basis. Never jump straight into item one.
16. **Write plain, one or two reading levels down. This is not marketing copy.** Keep the technical terms and simplify the sentence around them. A working data engineer wants dry, accurate and concise. Ask yourself "what are we trying to say?", then say it in fewer, smaller words where possible, without patronizing our technically sophisticated audience. See section 2, "Kill the clever declarative".
17. **No clever or provocative declarative sentences.** Do not try to sound smart while teaching the reader nothing. Each sentence must convey value-adding information. Say the plain thing instead. See section 2.
18. **Name every noun the reader needs.** No dangling referent. "All four write competent SQL" and "the best editor of the four" make the reader stop and ask "all four what". Name them in the sentence. See section 2, "Name every referent".
19. **Give an exact figure or a plain scope, never a vague count.** "13+ data platforms" makes the reader ask "is that 14 or 200". Prefer a plain-English scope such as "any data platform or cloud database", or a real number. Where the site-wide naming rule requires the platform list, name the platforms and drop the "+N" framing.
20. **One idea per sentence, and no internal contradiction.** Do not fuse two separate claims into one sentenc. Split the ideas and confirm they agree.
21. **No courtroom noun where a result belongs.** Added 25 Aug 2026 on the owner's report. "Verdict" is the current offender, in "it's not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation" and in "the verdict is still out". State the result, the number or the reason you cannot tell. The shape is banned and the bare word is not, because Altimate Code's PR review really does emit a signed verdict. See section 11.

The brand-safety gate `S2-*` in `check-listicles.mjs` enforces the framing half of rules 3, 4 and 12 as an
advisory warning. It is a floor. This list is the bar.

---

## 1. Substance decides the article

freeCodeCamp measures this and the finding is blunt: the deeper the piece, the longer people read it and the
more often they share it. Depth means facts, numbers, quotations, code and screenshots. It does not mean word
count, and padding a thin section to hit a target makes the article worse.

Every section answers one question a practitioner actually asks. If a section cannot carry a number, a command,
a config value, a failure mode or a named product behavior, the section has no reason to exist. Cut it and let
the neighboring section absorb the point.

Bring the evidence into the paragraph rather than gesturing at it. "Snowflake bills per-second with a
60-second minimum, so a warehouse that wakes for one 4-second query still charges you for 60" teaches the
reader something. "Snowflake billing has some subtleties" teaches nothing and costs a line.

## 2. Kill the filler transition

The single worst habit in this corpus is the standalone signpost sentence that carries no information:

| Delete | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "That is the gap a catalog server closes." | Announces a point instead of making it. The next sentence already makes it. |
| "Here is the honest limit." | Promises content, then defers it by a full sentence. |
| "Watch the split here." | Instructs the reader to pay attention rather than giving them something to pay attention to. |
| "Here is the practical version." | Implies the previous paragraph was impractical. |
| "Two things matter." | Counting is not content. Name both things. |

The repair is always the same: fold the information from the following sentence into the opening one, so the
paragraph starts by saying something. "A catalog server closes that gap by resolving a column name to the
definition your finance team agreed on, which is the one thing schema introspection cannot give an agent"
does the job of both sentences and leaves the reader with a fact.

A transition earns its place only when it carries new information: a contrast the reader would otherwise miss,
a scope limit, a causal link. "That trade holds only while the warehouse stays under four concurrent queries"
is a transition worth keeping, because it changes what the reader does next.

### Never write a sentence about the article

The worst version of the filler transition takes the page itself as its subject. It praises the writing's
fairness, announces that a point is about to be made plainly, or tells the reader how to feel about what
they are reading. It is always cuttable and it always reads as a writer defending a paragraph:

| Delete | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| "A fair comparison beats a hostile one." | Argues that the page is fair, instead of being fair. |
| "These are real strengths rather than a courtesy paragraph." | Defends the paragraph the reader is already in. |
| "The tables above are the most honest version we can publish." | Claims honesty rather than showing the provenance. |
| "The tradeoff is worth stating plainly." | Announces plainness, then delays it by a sentence. |
| "The permission model is worth naming." | Announces that a thing will be named. Name it. |
| "The spread is worth more than any headline." | Ranks your own findings for the reader. |
| "ours, and this page says so" | Talks about the page inside a data table. Write "ours, unaudited". |

The test is the subject of the sentence. If it is the page, the comparison, the table or the paragraph, cut
it and let the next sentence lead. Where the deleted sentence carried a real qualifier, move that qualifier
into the sentence that follows, so nothing factual is lost.

Navigation is the exception, and only when it delivers in the same breath. "Read the last row and the cheaper
model wrote nothing at all more than twice as often" points at a row and hands over the finding, so it earns
its place. "Read the table carefully" does not.

### Kill the clever declarative

Added 21 Aug 2026 from the LI-09 review. The second worst habit in this corpus is the short declarative
sentence that reaches for effect instead of a fact. It sounds like a closing line in an essay and it teaches
the reader nothing. The reviewer's own tell for it was reading the sentence and asking "what are you trying to
say?"

| Delete | Say instead |
|---|---|
| "The fourth row settles it." | "The last row changes the decision: the cheaper model returned nothing on 79 of 270 trials." |
| "Generation got cheap and verification did not." | "Model quality made SQL generation cheap. Checking that the SQL is correct did not get cheaper." |
| "An agent with no correctness layer moves work from writing to reviewing." | "An agent with no correctness layer shifts your effort from writing SQL to reviewing it." |
| "Reviewer attention is the scarcest resource on a data team." | "Your review time costs more than the licence, so wrong SQL is the expensive kind of output." |
| "Snowflake reached the same shape independently." | "The Snowflake team came to the same conclusion with its own benchmark." |

The repair is to keep the number and the mechanism and drop the flourish. If a sentence sounds quotable but you
cannot point at the fact inside it, it had no content.

### Name every referent

A sentence that omits the noun forces the reader to stop and resolve it. That is friction the reader pays and
you do not. Name the thing in the sentence that uses it.

| Delete | Say instead |
|---|---|
| "All four write competent SQL." | "Altimate Code, Claude Code, Cursor and Cortex Code CLI all write competent SQL." |
| "Cursor remains the best editor of the four." | "Cursor edits code better than the other three agents." |
| "Snowflake extended it beyond the warehouse." | "Snowflake extended Cortex Code CLI beyond the warehouse." |
| "A mixed estate benefits most because one install reaches every platform you connect." | "It is stack-agnostic, so one install connects to every data platform and database you run." |

The rule pairs with section 6: name the noun the first time, then reuse that exact name. A pronoun or a bare
count ("the four", "it", "13+") that a reader has to trace back is the same failure as an undefined term.

## 3. Paragraph depth over paragraph count

Altimate's guide caps a paragraph at four sentences. freeCodeCamp warns against walls of text. Neither one asks
for a page of one-line paragraphs, which is what a long run of two-sentence blocks produces: the eye skips, the
argument never accumulates, and the piece reads like generated text.

Aim for three to four sentences per paragraph in body prose. A paragraph should open with the claim, support it
with a number or a mechanism, then say what the reader does with it. Two-sentence paragraphs are for the
genuine pivot, not for every idea.

## 4. Headings say what the section delivers

Use "How to" and "What is" shapes, and avoid the -ing form. "How to Size a Warehouse Without Guessing" beats
"Sizing Warehouses". A heading is a promise, so the first paragraph under it has to pay that promise off
immediately rather than warming up to it.

Never write a colon in a heading. Never write a heading that only names a noun when the section is about an
action.

## 5. Active voice, second person, real commands

Write "you drop the warehouse one size and rerun the workload", not "the warehouse can be dropped one size".
Address the reader as "you" and address the tool by its name.

Every claim that a practitioner could test should come with the way to test it. A CLI command, a SQL query
against `SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE`, a config key with its default value, a file path. This is the difference
between an article a reader believes and an article a reader skims.

## 6. Define the term once, then reuse it exactly

Spell out an acronym the first time and never swap in a synonym afterwards for variety. Column-level lineage
stays column-level lineage. It does not become "field-level tracing" three paragraphs later. Synonym rotation
reads as fluent writing to the author and as ambiguity to the reader.

Load-bearing Altimate terms have fixed forms: context graph (lowercase), Decision Memory (capitalized),
the Three Questions in their fixed order, agent decision loop. The naming rules in the repo's `CLAUDE.md`
also bind here: "13+ data platforms" and never "13 warehouses", "Altimate Lite" and never "the Native App",
"1M+ installs" and never a raw figure.

## 7. Cite the source and link the reader to it

Quote directly when the wording matters, attribute the quotation to the person or the vendor who wrote it, and
link the page. Paraphrasing someone's argument closely without a link is plagiarism, and it also removes the
one thing that makes a claim checkable.

Competitor names appear in the prose and never as hyperlinks, per the site-wide rule enforced by gate
L8-competitor-link. The evidence still lives in the citation span maps under `review/citations/spans/`, which
review mode surfaces for internal reviewers.

## 8. Mechanical bar

These are checked, not judged:

1. `yarn listicle-check` and `yarn listicle-links` both return zero errors.
2. `python "D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\slop\score.py" "<file>"` returns CRIT 0.
3. Review mode reports zero readability flags at amber 8.
4. Every sentence carries a finite verb. No fragments, no staccato triples, no noun-phrase anaphora.
5. No em-dash, en-dash, double hyphen or semicolon anywhere in the prose.

> **UNRESOLVED-D-DRIVE, procedural.** Raised 21 Aug 2026. The slop scorer lives on one contributor's
> Windows machine, so nobody else can run it: not another author, not macOS, not CI. Every other item on the
> mechanical bar is checkable by anyone with the repo. This one is not, which means "passes slop at CRIT 0"
> is a claim only its author can make and nobody can verify. The same is true of `slop_rules.py`, cited as a
> source feeding this guide, whose contents no reviewer outside that machine has read. Resolve it by
> vendoring the scorer and its rules into a repo, or by removing it from the mechanical bar. Until then,
> treat a skipped slop run as an expected gap rather than a failure, and say so in the PR.

## 9. The test that outranks the rest

Two questions decide whether a paragraph stays.

Would this survive a competitor publishing the same page? If the paragraph only makes sense as Altimate
marketing, it belongs in the sidebar and not in the body.

Would a senior data engineer find this useful, or roll their eyes? A sentence that tells them something they
already know, in words that sound like a press release, fails on both counts.

## 10. No existence-assertions in place of claims

Never write that something "is real," "is genuine," "is legitimate," "isn't
just noise," or "is actually there."

That construction marks a spot where a specific claim belongs. Replace it with:
 - the number (effect size, magnitude, direction, sample, interval), or
 - the attribution ("three of five interviewees raised it"), or
 - a plain statement that you can't tell, and what would settle it.

Before finishing, scan the draft for this pattern and rewrite every instance.

Examples:
 "The difference in the data is real"
   → "Group B converted 4.1pp higher (12.7% vs 8.6%, n=1,840, p=.003)."
 "The difference in the data is real" [numbers unavailable]
   → "I can't separate that gap from variance at this sample size; it'd take
      roughly 2,000 sessions per arm."
 "The frustration is real"
   → cut the sentence, respond to the frustration.

Exception: technical senses of "real" are fine: real vs. nominal, real vs.
synthetic data, real numbers.

## 11. No courtroom nouns in place of a result

Reported by the owner on 25 Aug 2026 as the successor to the "is real" tic in section 10. It is the same
defect wearing a different word. A model reaches for a judgment noun where a plain result belongs, so the

- "So the honest answer is not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation."
- "It's not a verdict, it's a starting point."
- "The verdict on Fusion is still out."
- "That table delivers a verdict on both tools."

| Rejected | Shipped |
|---|---|
| It's not a verdict, it's a break-even calculation. | Which tool costs less depends on your query volume. Under 400 queries a day, Altimate Code is cheaper. |
| The verdict on Fusion is still out. | dbt Labs has published no Fusion benchmark on a project this size, so we cannot compare the two yet. |
| That table delivers a verdict on both tools. | The table shows one tool failing 4 of the 12 checks and the other failing 1. |

## 12. Earn the insight before making the claim

Migrated from the tone-of-voice guide, which is where this rule used to live. It is article structure, so it
belongs here.

The reader has to understand the problem before the solution appears. Jumping to the product is the most
common structural failure in this corpus.

1. Name the problem a practitioner recognises from their own work.
2. Quantify or illustrate it, with a number, a scenario or a code example.
3. Say what the existing approaches miss.
4. Introduce what Altimate does differently, and be specific.

## 13. Say what breaks, not that something matters

An adjective that ranks importance tells the reader you think a thing matters and never why, so they can

## 14. Length and format by content type

LinkedIn, press quotes and sales email.

| Content type | Length and format | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Listicle | 2,000 to 3,200 words, and the cap is a blocking gate. | Structure rules come from the listicle harness. |
| Blog post (concept or narrative) | 1,200 to 2,000 words. Section headers. One concrete CTA at the end. | Open on a practitioner scenario, not a market claim. End on a specific action. Prose in the body, not bullets. |

| Product release notes | 50 to 200 words per feature: what it does, why it matters, how to use it. | Functional and direct. Engineers are reading this. |

- **Public repo:** you paste a GitHub link and click **Audit it**. If the repo is already audited, the board opens. Otherwise a prefilled GitHub issue opens. A new GitHub Action then audits the repo, commits the result to the log and posts the board link on the issue.
- **Private repo:** the page shows three commands to copy. The first two install FirstRun and run `firstrun audit owner/repo` with the user's own git login, so nothing leaves their machine.
- **Getting a private audit onto the log (optional):** the third command, `firstrun audit-submit --open`, is new. It uploads the audit as a secret gist and opens the issue with the gist link filled in. The Action publishes it only after you add a `publish` label, because a gist cannot be checked against a repo it cannot read. You are the reviewer.

**Doc-test, top of page:** one input bar under the title. It accepts a docs URL or a share code. The share-code box at the bottom is gone.
- **Share code:** opens the replay.
- **Docs URL that is already tested:** shows its result and a replay button.
- **New docs URL:** shows the install and `firstrun <url>` commands.

I checked all of these flows in a headless browser at 1440px and 375px: no console errors and no sideways scroll. 295 tests pass, including 8 new ones for the intake.

**A test failure, fixed in this PR:** the secret-scan test failed on an AWS-key-shaped string. It came from screenshot image data inside an Entire session transcript, not from a real key. The test now scans only branches, tags and remotes, not Entire's checkpoint refs.

**Entire:** its commit hook hung again for over 3 minutes. I stopped only that hook process, and the commit went through.

Decision for you: should I merge PR #30? Before merging, I need to create two labels in the repo, `audit-request` and `publish`, because the issue form applies `audit-request` on open. Reply "merge" and I'll create both labels, merge, and check the live site.

"""Unit economics from neatlogs traces, and the per-tier cost cap the agent enforces.

`firstrun econ` reads every `firstrun.run` trace, writes business/drivers.csv for cfo.ai,
and writes business/unit_economics.json. `firstrun run --tier NAME` reads that file and
stops a run whose spend passes the tier's cap.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

from firstrun.models import Budget

BUSINESS = Path(os.environ.get("FIRSTRUN_BUSINESS_DIR", "business"))
NEATLOGS = ["npx", "--yes", "-p", "node@22", "-p", "neatlogs-cli@0.2.0", "--", "neatlogs"]
DEFAULT_MARGIN_FLOOR = 0.70


class EconError(Exception):
    pass


def fetch_traces(since: str) -> str:
    """Raw JSON from `neatlogs traces list`. Keys come from the environment, never printed."""
    cmd = [*NEATLOGS, "traces", "list", "--from", since, "--all", "--max-items", "300", "--limit", "50", "--json"]
    exe = shutil.which(cmd[0]) or cmd[0]
    env = dict(os.environ)
    for attempt in (env, {k: v for k, v in env.items() if k != "NEATLOGS_API_KEY"}):
        p = subprocess.run([exe, *cmd[1:]], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding="utf-8",
                           errors="replace", env=attempt, timeout=300)
        if p.returncode == 0:
            return p.stdout
    raise EconError(f"neatlogs traces list failed: {p.stderr.strip()[:300]}")


def run_traces(text: str) -> list[dict]:
    """The `firstrun.run` traces of a `neatlogs traces list --json` payload."""
    data = json.loads(text)
    traces = ((data.get("data") or {}).get("traces")) or []
    return [t for t in traces if t.get("traceName") == "firstrun.run"]


def _pick(values: list[float], q: float) -> float:
    """Nearest-rank quantile. Values must be sorted."""
    return values[round(q * (len(values) - 1))]


def drivers(traces: list[dict], vm_price_per_hour: float) -> dict:
    """Measured cost and duration per run, with the trace behind each quantile."""
    if not traces:
        raise EconError("no firstrun.run traces to measure")
    by_cost = sorted(traces, key=lambda t: float(t.get("totalCostUsd") or 0))
    costs = [float(t.get("totalCostUsd") or 0) for t in by_cost]
    secs = [float(t.get("durationMs") or 0) / 1000 for t in traces]
    mean_s = sum(secs) / len(secs)

    def at(q: float) -> dict:
        t = by_cost[round(q * (len(by_cost) - 1))]
        return {"usd": round(float(t.get("totalCostUsd") or 0), 5), "trace_id": t.get("traceId", "")}

    return {
        "traces": len(traces),
        "cost_mean": round(sum(costs) / len(costs), 5),
        "cost_p50": at(0.50),
        "cost_p90": at(0.90),
        "cost_p95": at(0.95),
        "cost_max": at(1.0),
        "duration_mean_s": round(mean_s, 1),
        "compute_per_run": round(vm_price_per_hour * mean_s / 3600, 5),
        "vm_price_per_hour": vm_price_per_hour,
    }


def tier_caps(d: dict, tiers: dict, margin_floor: float, costs: list[float]) -> dict:
605:    """Measure cost per run from neatlogs, write drivers.csv for cfo.ai and the per-tier cost caps."""

content.content:
def tier_caps(d: dict, tiers: dict, margin_floor: float, costs: list[float]) -> dict:
    """Per tier: the model spend one run may use and still keep the margin floor.

    A run that hits the cap every time still earns the floor, so the floor holds in the
    worst month. A tier with no revenue gets the measured median as its cap.
    """
    compute = d["compute_per_run"]
    costs = sorted(costs)
    out = {}
    for name, tier in tiers.items():
        price, runs = float(tier["price_usd_month"]), int(tier["runs_per_month"])
        if price <= 0 or runs <= 0:
            cap = d["cost_p50"]["usd"]
            rule = "no revenue, so the cap is the measured median run"
        else:
            cap = round(price / runs * (1 - margin_floor) - compute, 5)
            rule = f"revenue per run x (1 - {margin_floor:.2f}) - compute"
        over = sum(1 for c in costs if c > cap)
        row = {
            "price_usd_month": price,
            "runs_per_month": runs,
            "cap_usd_per_run": max(cap, 0.0),
            "cap_rule": rule,
            "measured_runs_over_cap_pct": round(100 * over / len(costs), 1),
        }
        if price > 0:
            rev = price / runs
            p95 = d["cost_p95"]["usd"] + compute
            row.update({
                "revenue_per_run": round(rev, 5),
                "margin_at_mean_pct": round(100 * (1 - (d["cost_mean"] + compute) / rev), 1),
                "margin_at_p95_pct": round(100 * (1 - p95 / rev), 1),
                "margin_at_old_cap_pct": round(100 * (1 - (Budget().cost_usd_per_run + compute) / rev), 1),
                "price_for_p95_at_floor": round(runs * p95 / (1 - margin_floor), 2),
            })
        out[name] = row
    return out


def build(trace_json: str, inputs: dict, margin_floor: float = DEFAULT_MARGIN_FLOOR) -> dict:
    traces = run_traces(trace_json)
    d = drivers(traces, float(inputs["vm_price_per_hour"]["value"]))
    costs = [float(t.get("totalCostUsd") or 0) for t in traces]
    return {
        "generated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
        "source": "neatlogs traces, traceName firstrun.run, list price not billed",
        "margin_floor": margin_floor,
        "drivers": d,
        "tiers": tier_caps(d, inputs["tiers"], margin_floor, costs),
    }


def write(econ: dict, out_dir: Path | None = None) -> list[Path]:
    """business/unit_economics.json and business/drivers.csv (the file Ari reads)."""
    out_dir = out_dir or BUSINESS
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    js = out_dir / "unit_economics.json"
    js.write_text(json.dumps(econ, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    d = econ["drivers"]
    src = f"neatlogs, {d['traces']} firstrun.run traces"
    rows = [
        ("traces_measured", d["traces"], "traces", "yes", src),
        ("cost_per_run_mean", d["cost_mean"], "USD", "yes", src),
    ]
    for q in ("p50", "p90", "p95", "max"):
        c = d[f"cost_{q}"]
        rows.append((f"cost_per_run_{q}", c["usd"], "USD", "yes", f"neatlogs trace {c['trace_id']}"))
    rows += [
        ("run_duration_mean", d["duration_mean_s"], "seconds", "yes", src),
        ("vm_price_per_hour", d["vm_price_per_hour"], "USD", "no", "AWS t3.medium on-demand, assumption"),
        ("compute_per_run", d["compute_per_run"], "USD", "no", "vm_price_per_hour x run_duration_mean / 3600"),
        ("margin_floor", econ["margin_floor"], "fraction", "no", "assumption, set by the founder"),
    ]
    for name, t in econ["tiers"].items():
        key = name.lower()
        rows.append((f"{key}_price", t["price_usd_month"], "USD per month", "no", "assumption"))
        rows.append((f"{key}_runs_per_month", t["runs_per_month"], "runs", "no", "assumption"))
        rows.append((f"{key}_cost_cap_per_run", t["cap_usd_per_run"], "USD", "no", t["cap_rule"]))
        rows.append((f"{key}_runs_over_cap_pct", t["measured_runs_over_cap_pct"], "percent", "yes", src))
    csv_path = out_dir / "drivers.csv"
    with csv_path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.writer(fh)
        w.writerow(["driver", "value", "unit", "measured", "source"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    return [js, csv_path]


def budget_for_tier(tier: str, path: Path | None = None) -> Budget:
    """The run budget with the tier's cost cap from business/unit_economics.json."""
    path = path or BUSINESS / "unit_economics.json"
    if not path.exists():

def tier_caps(d: dict, tiers: dict, margin_floor: float, costs: list[float]) -> dict:
    """Per tier: the model spend one run may use and still keep the margin floor.

    A run that hits the cap every time still earns the floor, so the floor holds in the
    worst month. A tier with no revenue gets the measured median as its cap.
    """
    compute = d["compute_per_run"]
    costs = sorted(costs)
    out = {}
    for name, tier in tiers.items():
        price, runs = float(tier["price_usd_month"]), int(tier["runs_per_month"])
        if price <= 0 or runs <= 0:
            cap = d["cost_p50"]["usd"]
            rule = "no revenue, so the cap is the measured median run"
        else:
            cap = round(price / runs * (1 - margin_floor) - compute, 5)
            rule = f"revenue per run x (1 - {margin_floor:.2f}) - compute"
        over = sum(1 for c in costs if c > cap)
        row = {
            "price_usd_month": price,
            "runs_per_month": runs,
            "cap_usd_per_run": max(cap, 0.0),
            "cap_rule": rule,
            "measured_runs_over_cap_pct": round(100 * over / len(costs), 1),
        }
        if price > 0:
            rev = price / runs
            p95 = d["cost_p95"]["usd"] + compute
            row.update({
                "revenue_per_run": round(rev, 5),
                "margin_at_mean_pct": round(100 * (1 - (d["cost_mean"] + compute) / rev), 1),
                "margin_at_p95_pct": round(100 * (1 - p95 / rev), 1),
                "margin_at_old_cap_pct": round(100 * (1 - (Budget().cost_usd_per_run + compute) / rev), 1),
                "price_for_p95_at_floor": round(runs * p95 / (1 - margin_floor), 2),
            })
        out[name] = row
    return out


def build(trace_json: str, inputs: dict, margin_floor: float = DEFAULT_MARGIN_FLOOR) -> dict:
    traces = run_traces(trace_json)
    d = drivers(traces, float(inputs["vm_price_per_hour"]["value"]))
    costs = [float(t.get("totalCostUsd") or 0) for t in traces]
    return {
        "generated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
        "source": "neatlogs traces, traceName firstrun.run, list price not billed",
        "margin_floor": margin_floor,
        "drivers": d,
        "tiers": tier_caps(d, inputs["tiers"], margin_floor, costs),
    }


def write(econ: dict, out_dir: Path | None = None) -> list[Path]:
    """business/unit_economics.json and business/drivers.csv (the file Ari reads)."""
    out_dir = out_dir or BUSINESS
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    js = out_dir / "unit_economics.json"
    js.write_text(json.dumps(econ, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    d = econ["drivers"]
    src = f"neatlogs, {d['traces']} firstrun.run traces"
    rows = [
        ("traces_measured", d["traces"], "traces", "yes", src),
        ("cost_per_run_mean", d["cost_mean"], "USD", "yes", src),
    ]
    for q in ("p50", "p90", "p95", "max"):
        c = d[f"cost_{q}"]
        rows.append((f"cost_per_run_{q}", c["usd"], "USD", "yes", f"neatlogs trace {c['trace_id']}"))
    rows += [
        ("run_duration_mean", d["duration_mean_s"], "seconds", "yes", src),
        ("vm_price_per_hour", d["vm_price_per_hour"], "USD", "no", "AWS t3.medium on-demand, assumption"),
        ("compute_per_run", d["compute_per_run"], "USD", "no", "vm_price_per_hour x run_duration_mean / 3600"),
        ("margin_floor", econ["margin_floor"], "fraction", "no", "assumption, set by the founder"),
    ]
    for name, t in econ["tiers"].items():
        key = name.lower()
        rows.append((f"{key}_price", t["price_usd_month"], "USD per month", "no", "assumption"))
        rows.append((f"{key}_runs_per_month", t["runs_per_month"], "runs", "no", "assumption"))
        rows.append((f"{key}_cost_cap_per_run", t["cap_usd_per_run"], "USD", "no", t["cap_rule"]))
        rows.append((f"{key}_runs_over_cap_pct", t["measured_runs_over_cap_pct"], "percent", "yes", src))
    csv_path = out_dir / "drivers.csv"
    with csv_path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.writer(fh)
        w.writerow(["driver", "value", "unit", "measured", "source"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    return [js, csv_path]


def budget_for_tier(tier: str, path: Path | None = None) -> Budget:
    """The run budget with the tier's cost cap from business/unit_economics.json."""
    path = path or BUSINESS / "unit_economics.json"
    if not path.exists():
        raise EconError(f"{path} not found. Run `firstrun econ` first.")
    tiers = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["tiers"]
    match = {k.lower(): v for k, v in tiers.items()}.get(tier.lower())
    if match is None:
        raise EconError(f"unknown tier {tier!r}. Known: {', '.join(tiers)}")
    return Budget(cost_usd_per_run=float(match["cap_usd_per_run"]))

target.description: The built-in skill's name, exactly as skills reports it.

Skills to read, each named exactly as skills reports it. A name matching nothing does not fail the call: unmatched names are listed in a trailing unresolved entry with candidate skills this workspace holds.

schema9.description: Case-insensitive name filter; absence includes all names.

input_schema.description: Fill exactly one action block: file, instructions, list, read.

entries.name: mcp__cfoai__inspect_table_blocks
entries.description:
Input constraint: Provide parameters for exactly one of: (bounds) or (compare) or (dimension) or (items) or (list) or (read) or (variable).

Lists saved tables (a summary each, or the full layout of tables named in target), reads selected cells, or compares saved states. One read returns several scenarios side by side when comparison names them. Rows and columns are objects with reusable refs. Rows carry formulas by range, bare values in column order, writability, and hidden-child counts; cell exceptions carry value and cell_formula. Columns carry the variable or dimension, grain, and date range; ranges defines each range once. Rows and columns are selected by inspected ref, unambiguous name, or coordinate predicate; depth controls descendants. include_edit_rules adds owned defaults and accepted actions. items and bounds inspect a dimension with or without a table target. references names the properties returned formulas use. variable and dimension inspect named objects and their dependents, or list them all. Unreadable evidence stays explicit. Reads never change the model. Omitted format uses json; an explicit format overrides it for this call.

_context.description: Optional active scenario, page, and time zone.

before_change_log_id.description: The earlier saved change to compare against. The comparison names rows removed or added since it under row_membership.

page.description: Limit a table list to this existing page.

target.description: Saved tables by name or ref, one or a list. Named tables come back in full: layout, signature, presentation, and property homes. Omission lists every table as a summary of row and column counts, first rows, and window; names that match nothing are reported under unresolved.

org_id.description: Workspace ID or slug. Optional when you belong to one workspace. Otherwise, call list_orgs and choose an ID or slug. Numbers always identify workspace IDs.

measures.description: Values per compared scenario: VALUE, DELTA (difference from the selected scenario), PERCENT (percent difference). Defaults to VALUE.

scenarios.description: Existing scenarios to read beside the selected scenario, by name or inspected reference.

comparison.description: For action read. saved uses the saved comparison; none reads underlying values and formulas; an object compares the selected scenario with each named scenario in this one read, whatever the table saves. Defaults to saved. The saved table is unchanged.

grain.description: Reads the table's Date periods rolled up to this coarser grain without changing the saved table; the grain the table already shows is its plain read. Each period holds what the model calculates at that grain: a variable's time rollup (its base periods summed, closed, or averaged) or a timeless formula recomputed there; a variable with neither reads blank. Rolled-up period columns are read-only; the saved table's own columns take writes.

recalculate.description: Calculates the table from scratch, ignoring every cached or reused result, and makes that calculation the cached one so the page shows it too. Use it when a value disagrees with what the person sees, with another read, or with arithmetic you can check; the result's recalculated says whether the cached result differed. Needs comparison none: a saved or requested comparison refuses it. Costs a full calculation; not for routine reads.

scenario.description: Scenario to use. Defaults to the scenario in view, which can change between turns.

after.description: The previous page's next.after; it continues the same target, or the listing at the object and definition where that page stopped, at the same snapshot.

after_2.description: Grid continuations bind table, selection, scenario and snapshot. Focused next binds its definition page and snapshot. For items, copy the prior member spelling, including an empty string. For list, copy next.after.

as_of_point.description: Optional snapshot with exactly one point type. Absence selects the current state.

calendar_boundary.description: A local calendar period boundary in the user's runtime timezone, for phrases such as "yesterday" or "last month"; UTC when no timezone is known.

offset.description: 0 is the current period, -1 the previous, 1 the next.

change_log_id.description: Exact or approximate changelog point. The backend resolves to this workspace's latest changelog at or before this ID.

relative_duration.description: A duration from now, such as "a couple hours ago" or "a day from now"; a day is 24 hours and a week is seven days.

timestamp.description: Exact instant supplied by the user, runtime context, or a tool result, as RFC3339 or RFC3339Nano with a timezone.

columns.description: Column references as a read prints them, unambiguous names, a member by its path from its variable or its axis dimension, one bracket per breakdown level, or native coordinate predicates; a name in backticks selects the same column as the name without them. Omission includes the saved columns; explicit columns take precedence over periods.

period_range.description: Inclusive system Date interval at the saved axis grain, with bounds in that grain's period spelling, such as 2026-07 through 2026-09 for month.

conditions.description: Filter stored formula definitions by readable conditions. Omission includes every saved definition.

depth.description: Descendant levels relative to selected rows, or saved roots when rows are omitted. With rows, omission returns those rows only; without rows, omission leaves the full saved tree eligible.

dimension.description: Existing workspace dimension by name or inspected reference, including imported dimensions before table placement.

format.description: Optional compact JSON or addressed REAM encoding override. Omission uses the workspace's current default encoding.

formula_origins.description: Each row or column already carries its formula per range under formulas, a cell that breaks that rule says so in the cell, and a row or column computed by a rule saved outside this table's nodes names that rule's owner and condition in inherited_from. Omission is off; a selection of exactly one cell defaults to all. zeros adds rules to rows containing a zero, blank, or error: every rule the engine ranked for the row, best first, with the ones that computed a cell marked selected. all adds rules to every row.

include_edit_rules.description: Adds each returned row's and column's editing rules: the actions the edit input accepts there, its owned Actuals and Forecast defaults with ownership and writability, and its formula roles. Omission returns writability alone; a refused write reports the rules it broke.

include_inputs.description: Expands one level of formula inputs beneath the selected rows. With one cell selected by rows and columns and comparison none, also explains its input values and sources. Input rows and evidence share the response budget.

limit.description: Saved formula definitions per page, default 100. A scope can span pages; next continues it. An oversized formula returns unavailable coverage instead of truncated text.

limit_2.description: Maximum grid rows, items, or listed tables (500), or saved formula definitions (100). Defaults: grid 500, items 50, tables 100, formula definitions 100. Grid parents and descendants count separately. The response budget may stop earlier; calculation inputs stay complete.

periods.description: boundaries returns only the first and last period of each range (where Actuals end and Forecast begins) and of the window, without changing the saved table. An explicit column selection takes precedence.

rows.description: Row references as a read prints them, unambiguous names or full paths, a member by its path from its variable or its axis dimension, one bracket per breakdown level (Revenue[West], Revenue[West][Enterprise], Employee ID[E-207], and Revenue[empty:None] for the member with no value), or native coordinate predicates; a name in backticks selects the same row as the name without them. Matches are deduplicated in saved order. Omission leaves the saved tree eligible. A read that names rows or columns holds every member of the layout, zero and empty members included, whatever the saved display hides; a read that names none shows what the app displays.

period_range.description: Inclusive system Date interval at the saved axis grain, with bounds in that grain's period spelling, such as 2026-07 through 2026-09 for month.

scenario.description: Scenario to use. Defaults to the scenario in view, which can change between turns.

source_health.description: Source status detail. Compact is the default.

target.description: Optional saved table that must contain the dimension. Without it, the read covers imported or manual members before any table exists.

target_2.description: A workspace-wide variable or dimension reference, or a list of them, including at a historical snapshot. A list answers with one entry per reference in the order given, each source query stated once under sources, and a reference that matches nothing refused in its own entry. Omission lists every readable variable or dimension in the scenario as the same entries, in saved order, with next continuing the listing.

input_schema.description: Fill exactly one action block: bounds, compare, dimension, items, list, read, variable. Fields beside the block apply to it: scenario.

entries.name: mcp__cfoai__inspect_triggers
entries.description: Reads the current user's scheduled Ari triggers: their instructions, schedules, enabled state, and last run. Other users' triggers cannot be read. last_dispatch_status describes a run that was attempted or started; only last_succeeded_at_utc proves completed work. Overlapping runs can be skipped.

_context.description: Optional active scenario, page, and time zone.

org_id.description: Workspace ID or slug. Optional when you belong to one workspace. Otherwise, call list_orgs and choose an ID or slug. Numbers always identify workspace IDs.

query.description: Case-insensitive name filter; absence includes all names.

entries.name: mcp__cfoai__list_orgs
entries.description: List your workspaces, including each ID, name, slug, and your role. Use an ID or slug as org_id for another tool. Tools select your workspace automatically when you belong to only one.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

- **Incidents:** neatlogs monitors every run, surfaces failures, and groups related cases into a single incident.
- **Investigation:** Its investigation flow finds the failure, adds the missing business context, isolates the likely cause, prepares the fix brief, and checks whether the change worked.

content.content:
# Build the model

A workspace has one model, and every table is a view of it. This skill starts with the picture of
how the engine computes a model, told on one running example, then builds that example as the
calls that make it, then the engine's detail for imported records, mappings, and which rule fills a
cell. The rest is the business the model simulates: what it earns, what it costs, who does the
work, where cash lands, and the statements that read from all of it.

## The model and its views

A variable's name, formulas, and values are the model, shared by every table that shows it.
Ordering, formatting, and the breakdown a table shows are the view, owned by that table. A change to
an existing table keeps its block identity and edits it in place; a copy on another page is a
separate block with the original left alone.

A readable name identifies an object only together with its identity: two variables can carry one
name, and the token an inspection or receipt prints, such as `Headcount#7d3`, names exactly one.
A name that matches an existing variable reuses that variable, and a rule written through the new
row replaces the rule every table reads. The existing object is the one to reuse when it is the one
the request means; a requested report keeps the names the request gives its variables, even when an
unrelated object already has such a name (`new: true` on the create), and keeps the shape the
request spells out: breakdown dimensions in the order listed, each listed field a column. A
different name or shape is a different deliverable. Saved data, research, supplied numbers, and
disclosed assumptions all build, and the missing variables and dimensions the work needs are yours
to create.

A table owns the variables and dimensions first created on it, its home, so deleting the table
deletes them and breaks every rule and table that reads them; a table whose objects others use
stays, or its objects move first to the table that stays. Tool calls in one turn run at the same
time, so a call that needs another's result, a variable a create makes or a member an update adds,
waits for it, and one create carries a table with its rules.

## The picture

The running example is a listening service. It sells two tiers, Lark and Chorus, in two territories,
Southgate and Eastmere, and is modeled month by month. Five ideas carry the engine.

### A cell

A cell is one variable at one member of each of its dimensions, and at one period when the variable
is dated. Paying listeners for Chorus in Eastmere in March 2027 is one cell. Tier fee for Chorus is
a timeless cell: it has a tier and no month. A table shows some of a variable's cells; the cells
exist wherever the variable's rules and inputs reach.

### A rule and an input

A cell holds a literal input or a formula. An input is a supplied fact or a chosen assumption,
and its cell is the customer's control: an opening count, fee, or growth rate. A formula calculates
from inputs at each cell's coordinates and keeps its dependencies even when today's answer is constant.
Its condition names the Date grain: a Month rule reaches additional business dimensions at Month;
a daily forecast needs matching Day coverage, and time conversions are explicit calculations.
Actuals and Forecast are separate range choices. The saved scope and selected rule explain coverage;
a literal such as months in a year is part of the rule.

A forecast reads earlier cells. A dated input carries forward through an opening cell and a
default formula for later periods, so every later month depends on the assumption. Repeated literals
would create independent overrides. Weekly listeners grow from an opening input:

```formula
`Weekly listeners`[-1] * (1 + `Listener growth`$[Territory = this.Territory])
```

In the first Forecast month, `Weekly listeners[-1]` is the last Actuals month, so it reads that
month's input, imported value, or Actuals rule; with none of them it reads 0, and every later month
compounds from 0. A model with no connected actuals seeds the opening input in its last Actuals
month. For cash, the opening cell holds the starting amount and the default adds Net Cash Flow to
the prior balance. A recurrence reads its previous period's modeled value: its selected rule, or the
source or zero fallback. An estimated opening stays distinct from observed history, and a legitimate
zero, such as payroll before a hire starts, stays zero.

An intentional one-cell override pins that cell and nothing else; removing it lets the default's
value flow into parents and rollups, so the neighboring periods and parents are what to read
afterward.

An empty read has one rule. An aggregate over no matching cells returns that function's empty
result: `sum` and `product` 0, `min`, `max`, and `average` null. A variable cell with no rule and no
input reads null for a date or text and 0 for any other type, so an End Date nobody entered is null,
and `End Date = null` is true there. A blank imported number is null in the source; a SUM variable
over a record whose rows are all blank reads 0, so `count` over that variable counts the cell, while
`last(<column>)` over the same rows reads null and `count(<column>)` on the raw column counts no
blank. `a = null` asks
whether a value is missing; `a = b` is null when either side is missing, so `if` takes its false
branch, and an unassigned group matches two missing attributes with `(a = null and b = null) or a =
b`. A ratio states its error fallback, ``iferror(`Listening revenue` / `Paying listeners`, NULL)``.

.....

## Scenarios

Mutually exclusive business futures are scenarios. Additive dimension items coexist in one future
and their aggregate answers a real question; a total across alternative fundraising or growth cases
answers nothing, so alternatives are scenarios and the model's dimensions are the coordinates the
business actually has. A scenario inherits unchanged state from its base. User-authored overrides
are scenario-scoped; imported source records stay shared and read-only.

A write with no `scenario` lands in the scenario the person is viewing, which can change between
turns; a write meant for another scenario names it. A lever that moves only the forecast is a dated
input whose Forecast cells differ in the scenario, or an input only the Forecast rule reads: Upside
overrides Listener growth, which only the Forecast rule of Weekly listeners reads. A timeless value
that every period reads moves the history too, because a scenario can change closed periods as well.
Cases sit side by side in one table through its `comparison` with `scenarios`. Each comparison column identifies a period and a scenario: Main's September 2027 column and Upside's September 2027 column have separate returned refs. Selecting the inspected Upside ref reads that case's value.
A read of the selected scenario with `comparison: "none"` inspects its underlying model values and formulas while keeping the table's saved comparison. On an underlying read, `formula_origins: "all"` adds annotations showing which rules computed its cells. Comparison values can be complete while the selected formula is reported as unavailable.
A Canvas simulator shows one scenario at a time unless cross-scenario Canvas reads are enabled for the workspace.

## What a saved value proves

The calculated readback tells a no-data blank from a numeric zero. A write receipt whose `status` is
`applied`, with its `changed` counts and readback, proves the change, and the receipt states what
the write replaced, tied, or refused, so the next call can be shaped from it. When a receipt cannot
prove the outcome, the saved table is read at meaningful starting and later periods, business
segments, and coarser grains. Verify a saved read on system Date at the requested grain with a
member whose state changes inside the window: a start, an end, a rate change, a different currency.
A member that never changes cannot reveal a wrong read, and an undated total cannot prove the
projection.

A saved value proves that the rule computes at those coordinates; a member whose value follows from
its own record, a salaried member's full month equal to its rate divided by twelve, proves the
amount, and a cell that differs from its record is unfinished work. A result that differs from the
intended model traces to the selected rule and what its references read, and the breakdown stays
while the rule is repaired. A driver test proves how a result responds: after an input change,
compare the affected and the unaffected results at the requested grains.

A row blank or zero across the whole horizon is unfinished work unless the business fact is zero.
Say which checks ran and which relationships stay untested. A read that timed out proves nothing,
and the work stays unverified until a read returns. Missing scope, a wrong regime, a source column
placed at the wrong date, and unmapped items are modeling conditions, resolved in the model while
the imported rows stay as they are; the work is finished when the requested cells compute from the
source for the members whose state changes inside the window, and rows the source never contained
are the only evidence gap to report. The `variable` and `dimension` reads list what depends on an
object; a delete without `force` is refused while anything does and deletes at once when nothing
does; `force` is for a deletion the person asked for after hearing them. An edit to past periods is said so.
